Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
Carlos, a 54-year-old Latin American business owner, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on edge in ways that seemed to circle back on themselves. Years earlier, when he had worked as a relief worker in a war zone, he had been sent into neighborhoods after shelling to help distribute food and medical supplies. One afternoon, as he knelt beside a damaged clinic entrance to lift a box of bottled water, gunfire cracked close enough that he felt the sharp, physical force of danger in his chest; a frightened child pressed against him in the narrow doorway, and for a few seconds he was trapped in intimate proximity to other bodies while trying to keep moving. He survived, but afterward he could not stop replaying the moment in his mind. Over and over he went back to the question of why it had happened to him, as if there were a hidden answer he could find if he kept turning it over. What troubled him most was that his own sense of alarm had not only followed obvious threat, but had also become tangled with moments that should have been good or relieving. In the months that followed, even positive emotions felt wrong to him; if he laughed with his wife, enjoyed a family dinner, or felt a brief lift at work, he would become uneasy, almost suspicious of the feeling, as though something terrible might be waiting behind it.

Those reactions began to shape how Carlos moved through his days as a business owner. He kept a weapon with him, telling himself that if he stayed prepared, he would never again be caught helpless the way he had been abroad. He also found himself picking arguments, needling customers, and creating drama with employees when the atmosphere was calm, partly because agitation felt more familiar than peace and partly because it gave him somewhere to put the energy he could no longer contain. The moments that set this off were often small and ordinary: a loud pop from a car backfiring in the parking lot outside his shop, someone standing too close in line, a coworker reaching past him unexpectedly, or the sudden warmth of a family celebration that should have felt good. Each time, the body memory of the war zone seemed to rush in with it, and his immediate response was to sharpen his vigilance, keep the weapon close, and stir up conflict before his thoughts could settle on the trauma again. Yet the arguments and the constant readiness only fed the very sensations he feared. The more he armed himself and picked fights to distract himself, the more alert and reactive he became, scanning for the next sound, the next person moving too near, the next surge of confusing good feeling that made him brace for danger.

At home, his wife noticed that he could not simply enjoy a quiet evening anymore. If she tried to share pleasant news, he sometimes became irritable or abruptly suspicious, and he would later pace the house, replaying the old convoy route, the clinic doorway, and the feeling of bodies too close around him. In his shop, he was less patient with customers and more likely to provoke an exchange when things were too peaceful. He told himself that being on guard was the only reason he had made it through the war, and that letting his attention soften would leave him exposed again. That belief kept him moving between rumination and action: he would ask himself, again and again, why the event happened to him, and when the question became unbearable he would reach for the gun in his pocket or invent a dispute to break the tension. But the strategy never gave him real relief for long. Instead it made him more likely to notice every loud noise, every sudden closeness, and every moment of unexpected happiness as a warning sign. Even now, when he laughs with his wife and then feels a jolt of unease, he assumes something bad must be coming, and the old cycle of checking, arming, and arguing begins again.

By the time he sought help, Carlos was exhausted by how much of his life had narrowed around staying prepared. He had come after a particularly frightening afternoon at his business, when a sharp bang from the back lot sent him rushing to the door with his weapon in hand, and he realized how quickly he was being pulled back into the war zone in his mind. He is most afraid that if he cannot stop himself from staying armed, arguing, and replaying the past, he will lose his marriage and eventually become the kind of man who can no longer trust even a good moment. At the same time, he is hoping for a way to feel safe without having to keep the whole world at arm's length.
